title: Ledger
description: Class 11 Accountancy: meaning of the ledger, the posting process from journal to ledger, balancing of accounts (debit/credit balances), and preparing ledger accounts from journal entries with worked T-accounts.

topics.title: Meaning of Ledger and the Posting Process
topics.concept:
The journal records transactions in date order, but it cannot quickly tell us "how much cash do we have?" or "how much does Ram owe?" For that we need the ledger — the book of accounts, also called the book of final entry or the "king of the books." It collects together, at one place, all entries relating to each account.

Each account in the ledger has a T-shape: the left side is the debit (Dr) side, the right side is the credit (Cr) side. The standard format has columns for Date, Particulars, J.F. (journal folio) and Amount on each side.

Posting is the process of transferring entries from the journal to the ledger. The rules are simple and mechanical:

  • The account debited in the journal is posted on the debit side of its ledger account, written as "To [the other account]."
  • The account credited in the journal is posted on the credit side of its ledger account, written as "By [the other account]."

So if the journal entry is "Furniture A/c Dr 20,000 / To Cash A/c 20,000," we post "To Cash 20,000" on the debit side of the Furniture account, and "By Furniture 20,000" on the credit side of the Cash account. The same amount appears in two accounts, on opposite sides — that is double entry in action.

examples.problem: Example 1: Why is the ledger called the 'book of final entry'?
examples.solution:
It comes after the journal.

  • Transactions first go to the journal (original entry).
  • They are then posted to the ledger, the final place where each account is gathered.
examples.answer: Because transactions reach it only after the journal — it is where each account is finally collected.

examples.problem: Example 2: The entry is 'Salary A/c Dr / To Cash A/c'. On which side of the Cash account is it posted, and with what wording?
examples.solution:
Cash was credited.

  • Cash is credited → post on the credit side.
  • Wording: 'By Salary A/c'.
examples.answer: On the credit side of the Cash account, written as 'By Salary A/c'.

examples.problem: Example 3: What does the word 'To' indicate in a ledger account?
examples.solution:
Debit-side wording.

  • 'To' is written before items appearing on the debit side of an account.
examples.answer: It marks an entry on the debit side of the account ('By' marks the credit side).

recap:
• Ledger = book of accounts / book of final entry; each account is a T (Dr left, Cr right).
  • Posting: account debited in the journal → debit side ('To…'); account credited → credit side ('By…').
  • Every amount appears in two accounts on opposite sides (double entry).

quiz.q: The ledger is also called the book of:
quiz.explanation: The ledger is the book of final entry; the journal is original entry.

quiz.q: On the debit side of a ledger account, entries begin with the word:
quiz.explanation: 'To' is used on the debit side; 'By' on the credit side.

topics.title: Balancing of Accounts
topics.concept:
After posting, each account is balanced to find out how much is left in it. Balancing means totalling both sides and finding the difference.

The steps:

  1. Total the debit side and the credit side roughly (in the mind/margin).
  2. Find the difference and write it on the shorter side as "Balance c/d" (carried down) so that both sides become equal.
  3. Total both sides (they now match) and rule them off.
  4. Bring the balance down on the opposite side as "Balance b/d" (brought down) — this is the opening balance for the next period.

The nature of the balance tells us about the account:

  • A debit balance (debit side bigger) appears in assets, expenses and the drawings account. (Cash, debtors, machinery normally have debit balances.)
  • A credit balance (credit side bigger) appears in liabilities, capital and income accounts. (Creditors, capital, bank loan normally have credit balances.)

Two practical notes: (i) Nominal accounts (expenses/incomes) are usually not balanced — they are closed by transfer to the Trading or Profit & Loss Account at year-end. (ii) An account whose two sides are equal has a nil balance and needs no balancing.

examples.problem: Example 1: A Cash account has debit total Rs 90,000 and credit total Rs 65,000. What is the balance and its nature?
examples.solution:
Debit side is bigger.

  • Balance = 90,000 − 65,000 = 25,000.
  • Debit side bigger → debit balance (an asset).
examples.answer: A debit balance of Rs 25,000 (cash in hand).

examples.problem: Example 2: Where is 'Balance c/d' written, and why?
examples.solution:
On the shorter side.

  • It is written on the side with the smaller total.
  • This makes both totals equal so the account can be ruled off.
examples.answer: On the shorter (smaller-total) side, so that both sides become equal.

examples.problem: Example 3: Does a creditor's account normally show a debit or a credit balance?
examples.solution:
A liability.

  • A creditor is a liability (we owe them).
  • Liabilities have credit balances.
examples.answer: A credit balance (a creditor is a liability).

recap:
• Balancing: total both sides, put the difference on the shorter side as Balance c/d, then bring it down as Balance b/d.
  • Debit balance → assets, expenses, drawings. Credit balance → liabilities, capital, incomes.
  • Nominal accounts are closed (transferred to Trading/P&L), not balanced.

quiz.q: A debit balance is normally shown by:
quiz.explanation: Assets like cash have debit balances; creditors, capital and loans are credit balances.

quiz.q: The balance carried to the next period is brought down as:
quiz.explanation: Balance b/d (brought down) is the opening balance of the next period.

topics.title: Preparing a Ledger from the Journal
topics.concept:
Putting it together: given journal entries, we post each to the ledger and balance the accounts. Take three entries:

  1. Started business with cash Rs 50,000 → Cash A/c Dr / To Capital A/c.
  2. Bought goods for cash Rs 20,000 → Purchases A/c Dr / To Cash A/c.
  3. Paid rent Rs 5,000 → Rent A/c Dr / To Cash A/c.

The Cash Account collects everything touching cash:

Dr — Cash Account — Cr
To Capital A/c   50,000By Purchases A/c   20,000
 By Rent A/c   5,000
 By Balance c/d   25,000
50,00050,000
To Balance b/d   25,000 

The cash account shows a debit balance of Rs 25,000 (cash in hand). The other accounts are simpler — the Capital account has only "By Cash 50,000" (credit balance Rs 50,000), Purchases has "To Cash 20,000," and Rent has "To Cash 5,000."

This is the heart of book-keeping: journalise → post → balance. Once all accounts are balanced, the closing balances are listed in a trial balance — the subject of the next chapter — to check that the books agree.

examples.problem: Example 1: From the worked example, what balance does the Capital account show?
examples.solution:
Only one entry, on the credit side.

  • Capital A/c has 'By Cash 50,000' on the credit side.
  • So it shows a credit balance of Rs 50,000.

examples.problem: Example 2: After posting, the Cash account's debit total is 50,000 and credit postings are 25,000. What is the Balance c/d?
examples.solution:
Difference on the shorter side.

  • 50,000 − 25,000 = 25,000 on the credit side as Balance c/d.
examples.answer: Balance c/d Rs 25,000 (a debit balance brought down).

examples.problem: Example 3: What is the correct order of steps in book-keeping?
examples.solution:
Three steps.

  • Journalise the transaction, post it to the ledger, then balance the account.
examples.answer: Journalise → post to the ledger → balance the accounts.

recap:
• Post each journal entry to its ledger accounts, then balance them.
  • The Cash A/c gathers all cash receipts (Dr) and payments (Cr); its balance is cash in hand (a debit balance).
  • Flow: journalise → post → balance; closing balances feed the trial balance.

quiz.q: In the worked example, the Cash account's closing balance is:
The closing balances of all ledger accounts are listed in the:
quiz.explanation: A trial balance lists all ledger balances to check the books agree.

questions.q: The ledger is the book of:
questions.explanation: The ledger is the book of final entry.

questions.q: An individual account in the ledger is shaped like the letter:
questions.explanation: Ledger accounts use the T-format (Dr left, Cr right).

questions.q: Transferring entries from journal to ledger is called:
questions.explanation: Posting moves entries to the ledger.

questions.q: The account debited in the journal is posted on the ____ side of its ledger account.
questions.explanation: Debited account → debit side of its own account.

questions.q: Entries on the credit side of a ledger account begin with:
questions.explanation: 'By' is used on the credit side.

questions.q: Finding the difference between the two sides of an account is called:
questions.explanation: Balancing finds the difference between the sides.

questions.q: Balance c/d is written on the:
questions.explanation: It goes on the shorter side to equalise the totals.

questions.q: A cash account normally has a:
questions.explanation: Cash is an asset, so it has a debit balance.

questions.q: A creditor's account normally has a:
questions.explanation: A creditor is a liability — a credit balance.

questions.q: Assets and expenses normally have ____ balances.
questions.explanation: Assets and expenses show debit balances.

questions.q: Nominal accounts (expenses/incomes) are usually:
questions.explanation: They are closed by transfer to Trading/P&L, not balanced.

questions.q: The opening balance of the next period is shown as:
questions.explanation: Balance b/d (brought down) opens the next period.

questions.q: The correct order of book-keeping steps is:
questions.explanation: Journalise, then post, then balance.

questions.q: Cash A/c: Dr total 60,000, Cr postings 40,000. The balance is:
questions.explanation: 60,000 − 40,000 = Rs 20,000 debit balance.

questions.q: Ledger balances are summarised to check agreement in the:
questions.explanation: The trial balance lists all balances to verify agreement.

questions.q: For the entry 'Ram A/c Dr / To Sales A/c', how is the Sales account posted?
questions.explanation: Sales was credited, so post on its credit side as 'By Ram A/c' (the other account's name).

questions.q: A debtor's account shows Dr 12,000 and Cr 12,000. Its balance is:
options: Nil — the debtor has fully paid
questions.explanation: Equal sides mean a nil balance — the debt has been settled in full.

questions.q: Why is the Rent account NOT balanced at year-end but the Cash account is?
options: Rent is a nominal account, closed to P&L; Cash is real, carried forward
questions.explanation: Nominal accounts are transferred to Trading/P&L; real and personal accounts are balanced and carried forward.

questions.q: An account's debit side totals 75,000 and credit side 90,000. The Balance c/d and its position are:
options: 15,000 on the debit side (a credit balance)
15,000 on the credit side (a debit balance)
questions.explanation: Credit side is larger, so a credit balance of 15,000; Balance c/d is written on the smaller (debit) side to equalise.

questions.q: A capital account always tends to show a credit balance because capital is:
options: The firm's liability to the owner
questions.explanation: Capital is owed to the owner — a liability — so it carries a credit balance.

questions.q: If the cash payments in a period exceed the cash receipts plus opening cash, it suggests:
options: An error — cash cannot have a credit balance
questions.explanation: Physical cash can never be negative, so a credit balance in Cash signals a recording error.

questions.q: Posting the entry 'Drawings A/c Dr / To Cash A/c' affects the ledger as:
options: Drawings debit side 'To Cash'; Cash credit side 'By Drawings'
questions.explanation: The debited account (Drawings) gets a debit-side entry; the credited account (Cash) gets a credit-side entry.

questions.q: Why is the ledger more useful than the journal for answering 'how much does Ram owe?'
options: It gathers all of Ram's entries in one account and shows his balance
questions.explanation: The ledger groups all transactions of each account together, so a single balance answers the question.

questions.q: After balancing, an account shows 'To Balance b/d 8,000' on the debit side. This means the account has:
questions.explanation: Balance b/d on the debit side is a debit (opening) balance carried into the new period.

questions.q: A trial balance is prepared AFTER:
options: All accounts are posted and balanced
questions.explanation: Balances can only be listed once every account has been posted and balanced.
